text.en: Every apple and every grain of rice started as sunlight captured by a green leaf. The chloroplast is the tiny kitchen where this happens.

Plastids are double-membrane organelles of plants that make and store food; chloroplasts are green, chromoplasts are yellow, red or orange and leucoplasts are colourless.
A chloroplast has an envelope of two membranes, a stroma containing DNA and 70S ribosomes, and thylakoids stacked into grana joined by stroma lamellae.
Photosynthesis is the process in which green plants use sunlight, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and release oxygen.
6CO2 + 12H2O gives C6H12O6 + 6H2O + 6O2 in the presence of light and chlorophyll.
Chlorophyll a is the primary pigment at the reaction centre; chlorophyll b and carotenoids are accessory pigments that pass energy on to it.
Light reaction (Hill reaction, discovered by Robin Hill in 1939) occurs in the grana and converts light energy into ATP and NADPH + H+.
Dark reaction, the Calvin cycle, occurs in the stroma and uses the ATP and NADPH to reduce CO2 to carbohydrate; Melvin Calvin won the Nobel Prize in 1961.
Internal factors affecting photosynthesis include pigments and leaf age; external factors include light, carbon dioxide, temperature, water and minerals.
